name: Formalism for Formalism
description: Yura is a mathematician, and his cognition of the world is so absolute as if he have been solving formal problems a hundred of trillions of billions of years. This problem is just that! Consider all non-negative integers from the interval $$$[0, 10^{n})$$$. For convenience we complement all numbers with leading zeros in such way that each number from the given interval consists of exactly $$$n$$$ decimal digits. You are given a set of pairs $$$(u_i, v_i)$$$, where $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$ are distinct decimal digits from $$$0$$$ to $$$9$$$. Consider a number $$$x$$$ consisting of $$$n$$$ digits. We will enumerate all digits from left to right and denote them as $$$d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n$$$. In one operation you can swap digits $$$d_i$$$ and $$$d_{i + 1}$$$ if and only if there is a pair $$$(u_j, v_j)$$$ in the set such that at least one of the following conditions is satisfied: $$$d_i = u_j$$$ and $$$d_{i + 1} = v_j$$$, $$$d_i = v_j$$$ and $$$d_{i + 1} = u_j$$$. We will call the numbers $$$x$$$ and $$$y$$$, consisting of $$$n$$$ digits, equivalent if the number $$$x$$$ can be transformed into the number $$$y$$$ using some number of operations described above. In particular, every number is considered equivalent to itself. You are given an integer $$$n$$$ and a set of $$$m$$$ pairs of digits $$$(u_i, v_i)$$$. You have to find the maximum integer $$$k$$$ such that there exists a set of integers $$$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k$$$ ($$$0 \le x_i \lt 10^{n}$$$) such that for each $$$1 \le i \lt j \le k$$$ the number $$$x_i$$$ is not equivalent to the number $$$x_j$$$.
input_specification: The first line contains an integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \le n \le 50\,000$$$) — the number of digits in considered numbers. The second line contains an integer $$$m$$$ ($$$0 \le m \le 45$$$) — the number of pairs of digits in the set. Each of the following $$$m$$$ lines contains two digits $$$u_i$$$ and $$$v_i$$$, separated with a space ($$$0 \le u_i \lt v_i \le 9$$$). It's guaranteed that all described pairs are pairwise distinct.
output_specification: Print one integer — the maximum value $$$k$$$ such that there exists a set of integers $$$x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_k$$$ ($$$0 \le x_i \lt 10^{n}$$$) such that for each $$$1 \le i \lt j \le k$$$ the number $$$x_i$$$ is not equivalent to the number $$$x_j$$$. As the answer can be big enough, print the number $$$k$$$ modulo $$$998\,244\,353$$$.
approach_summary: Define state dp[mask][i] capturing the subset of visited/chosen elements. Transition by iterating over valid unset bits in O(2^N × N) time.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1679F — Formalism for Formalism [450. Bitmask DP]
topic_editorial.summary: Bitmask DP state compression over subsets.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because the dimension $N$ is small ($N \le 20$), each subset of chosen or visited elements can be encoded compactly into a single bitmask integer $0 \le \text{mask} < 2^N$. The optimal substructure property guarantees that to extend a subset $\text{mask}$, we only need to know the current subset and optionally the last added element.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: State Definition
Define $dp[\text{mask}]$ (or $dp[\text{mask}][u]$ if the last visited element matters) as:
- $dp[\text{mask}] = $ the optimal value obtainable using the subset of elements represented by the bitmask $\text{mask}$.

### Step 2: Base Cases
- Initialize all DP states to a sentinel value (e.g. $\infty$ for minimization, or $-\infty$ for maximization).
- Base state: $dp[0] = 0$ (empty configuration has cost zero).

### Step 3: Recurrence Relation & Transitions
For every mask from $0$ to $2^N - 1$:
If the state $dp[\text{mask}]$ is reachable:
For every element $i \in [0, N-1]$ such that the $i$-th bit is NOT set in $\text{mask}$ ($(\text{mask} \mathbin{\&} (1 \ll i)) == 0$):
$$\text{next\_mask} = \text{mask} \mid (1 \ll i)$$
$$dp[\text{next\_mask}] = \text{opt}\big(dp[\text{next\_mask}], dp[\text{mask}] + \text{cost}(\text{mask}, i)\big)$$

### Step 4: Final Answer
The final answer is stored in $dp[(1 \ll N) - 1]$, which corresponds to all $N$ elements being chosen.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N \cdot N)$
  There are $2^N$ total bitmasks. From each mask, we iterate over at most $N$ possible next bits to transition. For $N = 20$, $2^{20} \cdot 20 \approx 2 \times 10^7$ operations, which easily runs in $\approx 0.15$ seconds.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(2^N)$
  Storing the DP table for all $2^N$ configurations requires $2^{20} \times 8$ bytes $\approx 8\text{ MB}$ of memory, well below 256 MB.
